name: In-car and smart device announcements
h1: Short spoken announcements for devices, kiosks and in-vehicle apps
metaDescription: Add spoken status messages to connected devices, kiosks and vehicle apps with the ReadAloud API, called from a server, with caching and offline fallbacks.
intro: A device that talks needs messages that are short, predictable and reliable. A thermostat reports a fault, a kiosk announces a queue number, a fleet app tells a driver the next stop, a washing machine says the cycle is done. These devices share constraints that a web app does not have. They often have limited memory, spotty connectivity, a small speaker and no keyboard. Your key must not be embedded in firmware, so the device asks your server, and your server asks the speech API. That server-side design also gives you a place to cache. Most device announcements come from a small set of templates, so a clip rendered once can be stored and reused across thousands of devices. Connectivity decides the rest: if a message must be spoken when the network is down, bundle pre-rendered clips with the firmware and use live generation only for the variable parts. For a vehicle, driver-distraction and safety rules apply regardless of how good the audio is, and they are your responsibility, not the speech provider's.
steps: List every message the device can speak and split them into fixed phrases and templates with variables, such as a number or a place name.

Pre-render the fixed phrases with POST https://api.readaloudai.org/v1/audio/speech using readaloud-default, and choose wav, mp3 or opus to match your device's decoder. Request pcm if the device plays raw samples.
Bundle these clips into the firmware or app so the most important announcements work offline.
For variable messages, have the device call your own endpoint with the variable values. Your server builds the text, checks its cache, and otherwise requests audio from ReadAloud.
Return the audio with a cache header, and store it by text hash. Common values such as small numbers will be reused heavily.
Set a timeout and a fallback. If audio is not available within your limit, show the text on screen or play a short tone.
Test on the real speaker in the real environment, at engine and road noise, and adjust wording rather than only volume.

sampleExample.title: Fleet app prompt
sampleExample.input: Next stop, Cedar Street depot. Arrival in about six minutes. Please prepare the delivery list.
sampleExample.notes: Use ReadAloud Live, mp3 or opus depending on the device decoder. Pre-render fixed phrases; generate variable messages through your server with a one-shot request and cache by text hash.

whenToChooseReadAloud: You have a limited set of English messages and can pre-render most of them.
Your devices can reach a server of yours, and you can keep the key server-side.
You want formats such as raw pcm or opus that suit small devices.
You prefer a flat per-character price over a per-device licence: 200 characters is about $0.0008 on Live.
whenToChooseSomethingElse: The device must speak with no network at all and cannot bundle files; consider an on-device speech engine.
Drivers need hands-free, interactive conversation; use a full voice-agent platform and follow automotive safety guidance.
You sell in many countries and need local languages; look for documented per-language voices.
The product needs a distinct brand voice or an expressive character; that is beyond what Live offers.

featuresUsed.howItHelps: mp3, opus, wav and pcm cover most embedded decoders.
A server can generate clips with an existing OpenAI client after a base URL change.
Clients take your API key, so devices call your server, not ReadAloud directly.
Short announcements cost a very small fraction of a cent each.
Slowing a message slightly can help in a noisy cabin.

considerations: Driver-distraction rules, product safety standards and regional regulations apply to in-vehicle audio and are the maker's responsibility.
Disclose synthetic voice where rules require it, for example in product documentation.
Embed no API key in firmware or an app package; anyone can extract it.
The 5,000-character request limit is rarely an issue here, but a server's stream capacity can be, so cache heavily.

faq.q: Can the device call ReadAloud directly?
faq.a: Avoid it. The key would live on the device. Route requests through your own server.

faq.q: What if the device is offline?
faq.a: Bundle pre-rendered clips for the messages that matter, and fall back to text or tones for the rest.

faq.q: Which format suits a small microcontroller?
faq.a: Raw pcm is the simplest to play, at 24 kHz 16-bit mono on the OpenAI-compatible route. Check your device's memory and decoder.

faq.q: Can it announce in the driver's language?
faq.a: Only if you verify it. The documented voices are English, so this page does not promise other languages.

faq.q: Is the audio free to reuse across devices?
faq.a: Check ReadAloud's terms for output rights. Technically, a stored clip can be played any number of times without further charges.
